(1) the CRA is still valid, even in the case of the chimeric systems we discuss, (2) the CRA is not a mere thought experiment, but a valid argument, and (3) the CRA is relevant to the study of cognitive processes in biological and artificial systems alike.

understanding how cognition emerges in biological and artificial systems.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CRA is not a refutation of the computational theory of the mind, but it does show that the CRA does not apply to systems that are embodied, embedded, extended and enactive.

, even though the CRA may be overcome, it is still possible to argue that the mind cannot be equated with computation, but rather, that it is the body, and the body–brain interaction, that is crucial in the emergence of genuine understanding.
, in spite of the impressive technological advances, the CRA remains a powerful argument that shows that a purely syntactic account of cognition cannot account for genuine understanding.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are not yet in the position to understand the processes that give life to a mind.
, while the CRA is not a valid argument against the computational theory of the mind, it does provide a useful tool to identify and critique some of its most problematic assumptions.
, while the CRA does not apply to the chimeric systems we describe here, the same is not true for the biological systems that are the foundation for those systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the CRA, which is a thought experiment that has been used in the past to demonstrate the failure of the computational theory of cognition, can also be used to show the failure of attempts to blur the divide between biological organisms and artificial machines.
the CRA is still relevant to the study of cognition and the mind.
